In the [[2018 Birmingham City Council election|previous council election in 2018]], the first all-out elections in Birmingham, Labour maintained its control of the council, winning 67 seats. The Conservatives formed the main opposition with twenty-five seats, with the Liberal Democrats on eight and the [[Green Party of England and Wales|Green Party]] winning a single seat. In 2022, Labour maintained overall control. The Liberal Democrats and the Greens gained seats at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives. == Background == [[File:Birmingham Election Ward 2018.svg|thumb|Result of the 2018 council election]] The [[Local Government Act 1972]] created a two-tier system of metropolitan counties and boroughs covering [[Greater Manchester]], [[Merseyside]], [[South Yorkshire]], [[Tyne and Wear]], the [[West Midlands (county)|West Midlands]], and [[West Yorkshire]] starting in 1974. Birmingham is a district of the West Midlands metropolitan county.{{cite book |title=Local Government in England and Wales: A Guide to the New System |year=1974 |publisher=[[HMSO]] |location=London |isbn=0-11-750847-0 |page=7 }} The [[Local Government Act 1985]] abolished the metropolitan county councils, with the metropolitan boroughs individually taking on most of the county-level powers. The [[West Midlands Combined Authority]] was created in 2016 and began electing the [[mayor of the West Midlands]] from 2017, which was given strategic powers covering a region coterminous with the West Midlands metropolitan county.{{cite web|title=CONSTITUTION OF THE WEST MIDLANDS COMBINED AUTHORITY|url=https://www.wmca.org.uk/media/1576/constitution-master-module-2642017.pdf|access-date=4 December 2017}} Since its formation Birmingham City Council has variously been under [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] control, [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] control and [[no overall control]]. Councillors have predominantly been elected from the Labour Party, Conservative Party and the Liberal Democrats. The council has had an overall Labour majority since the [[2012 Birmingham City Council election|2012 council election]], when they regained control from the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition that had run the city since 2004.{{Cite news|date=2012-05-04|title=Labour gain control of Birmingham and Dudley councils|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-birmingham-17922884|access-date=2022-01-20}} In the [[2018 Birmingham City Council election|most recent council election in 2018]], Labour won 67 seats with 50.2% of the vote, the Conservatives won 25 seats with 28.8% of the vote, the Liberal Democrats won 8 seats with 14.1% of the vote and the Green Party won a single seat with 4.4% of the vote.{{Cite web|last=Rodger|first=James|date=2018-05-08|title=Every Birmingham local election 2018 result in full|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/birmingham-local-election-results-2018-14615464|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} The Labour councillor for Oscott Keith Linnecor died in February 2020, having served on the council for 25 years.{{Cite web|last=birminghammail.co.uk|date=2020-02-14|title=Touching tributes to much-loved Birmingham councillor after death|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/legend-friend-tributes-birmingham-councillor-17748755|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Cardwell|first=Mark|date=2021-04-29|title=Oscott by-election 2021 - Social housing and potholes|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/social-housing-potholes-among-oscott-20486800|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} Labour councillors for Billesley and Hall Green North, Lucy Seymour-Smith and Lou Robson, resigned.{{Cite web|last=Cardwell|first=Mark|date=2020-12-04|title=Third Brum council seat by-election likely for next year|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/third-birmingham-council-seat-election-19393289|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} The former Labour council leader [[John Clancy (Labour politician)|John Clancy]] also resigned his council seat in Quinton. Due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], all four by-elections were held in May 2021 alongside the [[2021 United Kingdom local elections|local elections across the country]] including the [[2021 West Midlands mayoral election|West Midlands mayoral election]]. The Labour candidates Katherine Carlisle and Saima Suleman were elected in Billesley and Hall Green North; while the Conservative candidates Darius Sandhu and Dominic Stanford made gains for their party in Oscott and Quinton.{{Cite web|last=Cardwell|first=Mark|date=2021-05-07|title=Full by-election results in Birmingham|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/full-election-results-birmingham-two-20550593|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} A Liberal Democrat councillor for Yardley East, Neil Eustace, died in September 2021. He had served on the council for 35 years.{{Cite web|last=Cardwell|first=Mark|date=2021-09-06|title=Tributes paid to 'dynamo' councillor who served for 35 years|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/tributes-paid-dynamo-birmingham-city-21498138|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} The Liberal Democrat candidate Deborah Harries successfully defended his seat in the October 2021 by-election.{{Cite web|last=Dare|first=Tom|date=2021-10-22|title=By-election results means Lib Dems gain an extra seat on the ward|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/birmingham-election-results-means-lib-21940180|access-date=2022-01-20|website=BirminghamLive|language=en}} The Labour MP for [[Birmingham Erdington (UK Parliament constituency)|Birmingham Erdington]] [[Jack Dromey]] died in January 2022. The Labour candidate [[Paulette Hamilton]] won the [[2022 Birmingham Erdington by-election|by-election held to fill the seat in March]], with an increased share of the vote.{{Cite news |date=2022-03-04 |title=Birmingham Erdington by-election: Starmer hails new MP as 'champion of working people' |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-birmingham-60613453 |access-date=2022-03-26}} The Labour councillor Zhor Malik defected to the Conservative Party in February 2022.{{Cite web |last=Lockley |first=Mike |date=2022-03-06 |title='Bullied' councillor claims Labour 'made his life hell' after switch to Tories |url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/they-made-life-hell-councillor-23302712 |access-date=2022-03-26 |website=BirminghamLive |language=en}} == Campaign == The Labour Party pledged to "treble" the number of speed cameras in the city if they were re-elected.{{Cite web |last=Richardson |first=Andy |date=2022-03-23 |title=Pledge to 'treble the amount of speed cameras in Birmingham' |url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/midlands-news/pledge-treble-amount-speed-cameras-23481885 |access-date=2022-03-26 |website=BirminghamLive |language=en}} The Liberal Democrats pledge to quadruple speed cameras, propose funding for up to 400 "walking bus conductors" and look to devolve the powers and resources of the council to more localised groups.{{Cite web |last=Dargue |first=Lee |date=2022-04-21 |title=Birmingham Local Elections 2022 - Liberal Democrat Manifesto |url=https://birminghamlibdems.org.uk/en/article/2022/1428766/birmingham-local-elections-2022-liberal-democrat-manifesto |language=en}} == Council composition == ===Prior to the election=== Birmingham City council has been controlled by the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] since [[2012 Birmingham City Council election|2012]]. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] last held sole control of the council in [[1984 Birmingham City Council election|1984]]. It was under no overall control from [[2003 Birmingham City Council election|2003]] until 2012, run by a Labour-[[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrat]] coalition from 2003 to [[2004 Birmingham City Council election|2004]] and by a Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition from 2004 to 2012.{{cite news|url=https://www.birminghampost.co.uk/news/local-news/eight-years-conservative-liberal-democrat-rule-3912264|title=Eight years of Conservative-Liberal Democrat rule in Birmingham|work=Birmingham Post|author=Neil Elkes|date=10 May 2012|access-date=25 January 2022}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! colspan="3" | After 2018 election ! colspan="3" | Before 2022 election |- ! colspan="2" | Party !
